scotus-california-vote-count.headline: Supreme Court rejects Trump's bid to stop California counting disputed votes
scotus-california-vote-count.body_md:
The Supreme Court has turned away the Trump administration's emergency request to make California set aside roughly 20,000 mail ballots that the Justice Department says come from "likely noncitizens." The order came on Monday, 2 November, the eve of the midterm elections. Counting continues as before. The ruling decides no question about who may vote. It settles only that the justices will not rewrite California's count while the case is still being litigated.

## What the court did

The order was one line and unsigned. Reports describe no noted dissents and no explanation. The court acted without asking California officials to respond. Reports differ on the mechanics: some say a single justice, Elena Kagan, denied the application without referring it to colleagues, and others describe it as an order of the court. Either way, no reasoning accompanies it, so it should not be read as a ruling on the merits.

That is the point of the emergency docket. The Justice Department did not ask the court to decide whether any particular person is a citizen. It asked for interim relief: segregate the flagged ballots now, sort out eligibility later. Its argument, as reported, was that once an unlawfully cast ballot is counted and commingled with lawful ones, the harm cannot be undone.

## How it got there

The Justice Department sued California on 15 October. It has lost at every stage since.

- **District court:** Judge David Carter rejected a temporary restraining order last week. He called the government's process for identifying alleged noncitizens "rife with uncertainty and errors," according to CBS News.
- **Ninth Circuit:** On 30 October a 2-1 panel declined to intervene. Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez wrote: "We decline the United States's invitation to contravene the Elections Clause by undermining the Constitution's plain text." They also said there is "no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals," and that the request likely violates the National Voter Registration Act's bar on systematic voter-list purges within 90 days of an election. Judge Patrick Bumatay, dissenting, called the proposal "a modest remedy."

State and county officials had warned that the federal list was unreliable, that eligible citizens could be disenfranchised, and that segregating ballots would push counting past California's 3 December certification deadline. California has more than 23 million registered voters, so 20,000 flagged people is a small fraction of the electorate. The dispute is about method and authority more than margin.

## Why the emergency docket is the story

The lower-court rulings leaned heavily on who runs elections: the Constitution's Elections Clause gives states the primary role in setting the manner of voting. The Supreme Court's refusal leaves that reading undisturbed for now, without endorsing it.

Timing also mattered. A change to counting procedure ordered days before an election, on the strength of a contested federal list, would have been a large intervention by a federal court in a state's administration of its own vote. The justices declined, and did so before the polls opened.

## What comes next

The underlying case, United States v. State of California, remains live. A hearing is reported for 13 November, according to local coverage; CBS did not mention one, so the date is worth confirming. Counting will largely be done by then, which raises a practical question: whether a court could order any remedy after the fact. The Justice Department's complaint also rests on its claim about the 20,000 names, which a court has yet to test on the evidence. California's certification deadline of 3 December is the next fixed point.

ehrc-reform-farage-column.headline: Equalities watchdog raises concerns with Reform over documentary remarks as Farage's Telegraph column ends
ehrc-reform-farage-column.body_md:
The Equality and Human Rights Commission, the statutory regulator for equality law in England, Scotland and Wales, has written to Reform UK about remarks made in an ITV undercover documentary. The letter asks the party what it is doing to comply with the Equality Act 2010. It is a request for information. The reports seen so far do not describe a formal investigation.

## What the regulator has asked

The EHRC said it had received complaints alleging unlawful activity under the Equality Act after the broadcast of *Undercover: A Year in Reform*. ITV's reporting on the film is dated 14 October. The watchdog's letter asks Reform to set out the steps it is taking to meet its obligations under the Act. The reports describe the concern as being about "racial and sexual remarks".

The programme, as reported by ITV and Reuters, showed Reform councillors and candidates making racist, sexual and violent remarks. One candidate was reported to have called Asian homeowners "parasites" and to have expressed anti-Muslim views. Two councillors who were later elected made sexually explicit comments about female Reform candidates. Reform MP Sarah Pochin was shown describing the party as "chauvinistic" and full of "alpha male shit".

One source dates the broadcast to September. The ITV coverage points to October, and that is the date used here.

## Reform's response

A Reform spokesperson said the party was confident it had complied with its Equality Act obligations and that there was "no room for racism in Reform UK". The party has said the individuals filmed are under investigation and have resigned or been suspended. It has also argued that not everyone captured on camera was a member. It reported ITV and the journalists involved to the police and has threatened civil action against the broadcaster. Nigel Farage has said the party's vetting of candidates has improved greatly.

The EHRC letter also sits alongside a separate approach. A group of Labour MPs led by Afzal Khan wrote to the commission alleging Islamophobia within Reform. That letter named several of the party's elected representatives and was not confined to the documentary. Reform's reply to it was: "We stand by our comments. We will not be intimidated." The coverage seen does not say whether the commission's letter relates to this complaint, to those about the film, or to both.

## Why a letter matters

The EHRC has powers to open inquiries and investigations, and to issue legally binding agreements or compliance notices. A request for information is the first and mildest step. It puts on record that the regulator has taken the complaints seriously enough to ask for answers. It does not make a finding. Whether the exchange stays at that level will depend on how detailed Reform's reply is, in particular on what it says about candidate vetting, training and complaint handling.

The politics are awkward for the party. Reform has built much of its appeal on being a challenger to established institutions, and its leadership has been quick to attack the broadcaster. A regulator asking about its internal conduct is harder to dismiss as a media story.

## The Telegraph column

The Guardian has also reported that Mr Farage's regular Telegraph column is to end. The material available gives no date, no reason, and no statement from the paper or from Mr Farage, so it is not clear whether the move is connected to the documentary row or is a routine change. It is better read as a separate development than as evidence of a breach with the paper.

## What to watch

The next marker is Reform's written reply to the EHRC and whether the commission publishes it or moves to a formal stage. Until then, the letter is a question to the party rather than a finding against it.

labour-greens-councils-split.headline: Labour ends power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row
labour-greens-councils-split.body_md:
Labour has ended power-sharing arrangements with the Green Party in 11 councils, according to BBC Politics, after a dispute over a Green motion describing Zionism as racism. The Bot Tribune has not been able to confirm the figure of 11 independently. The BBC report is the only source for it, and it gives no dates, councillors' names or quotes to show how far the break goes beyond those councils.

## How the row began

The split follows an ultimatum issued in mid-October. Labour's chair, Bridget Phillipson, wrote to local groups that share power with the Greens. She asked them to press their Green partners to reject the party's "Zionism is racism" policy. If the Greens did not respond within seven days, Labour said, it would end the arrangements.

Labour said the ultimatum affected 17 councils in England and one in Wales. Other outlets put the range at 17 to 19. Those figures cover every council where the two parties govern together, so 11 collapses would be a majority of them but not all. The reports reviewed do not say which 11 are meant.

## What has happened locally

Some outcomes are documented. In Lewes, the Green group said the two parties had "mutually agreed to end the alliance". In Sheffield, where Labour has 26 councillors and the Greens 19, the coalition was reported to be on the verge of collapse after the Greens declined to disown the motion. In Havant, the Greens stopped short of renouncing the policy but said they wanted to keep the coalition going.

The Greens are not united on the question. Dozens of Green councillors publicly distanced themselves from the policy after the ultimatum, according to Jewish News. That suggests the party's local groups are more divided than its conference position implies. The Liberal Democrats, who also share power with Labour in places, said it was for their local councillors to decide whether to end coalitions.

The equalities watchdog has also written to the Green Party to ask about the effect of the policy, according to ITV. That adds a regulatory strand to what began as a political quarrel.

## What it shows, and what it doesn't

The episode shows the Israel–Gaza dispute reaching the routine business of local government, where Labour and Green councillors have often worked together on housing, transport and budgets. Where the arrangements end, the usual result is a minority administration or a new deal with other parties, not an immediate change of control.

The national significance is harder to judge. Labour and the Greens compete for the same left-leaning voters, and a public break may harden that rivalry before future elections. But without a confirmed list of councils and dates, the evidence is of a series of local decisions rather than a single national realignment.

What to watch: the BBC's list of the 11 councils, if published, and the outcome in Sheffield, the largest of the arrangements at stake. Whether more Green groups follow the councillors who have disowned the motion will show if the remaining deals can be saved.

family-campaign-law-change.headline: Family of murdered girl given hope of law change
family-campaign-law-change.body_md:
A campaign led by the family of a murdered girl, who was killed by a former partner, has won the first signs that the UK government may be ready to change the law. That is the substance of a short BBC report. The report's headline says the family has been given hope, and the form of that hope is not set out in the material available to this desk.

That gap matters, and it is better stated than papered over. The details that would normally anchor a story like this could not be independently confirmed before publication: the girl's name, the date and circumstances of the killing, which law is at issue, and what, if anything, ministers have said on the record. Nothing here should be read as a confirmed government commitment. What can be said is narrower. A campaign focused on killings by former partners has produced movement that the BBC judged significant enough to report as a development.

## What is and is not known

The campaign centres on homicides committed by people who were, at the time, ex-partners of their victims. The BBC describes "signs of government movement" toward a change in the law. Movement is a soft word. In Westminster it can mean a minister agreeing to meet a family, a review being announced, an amendment being considered to a bill already before Parliament, or a firm promise of legislation. Those outcomes are very far apart, and the available reporting does not say which this is.

The reasonable reading, and it is an inference rather than a confirmed fact, is that the government has shown more openness than before, not that a law has been drafted. Campaigns of this kind usually advance in stages, and the first stage is almost always a change of tone.

## A familiar policy terrain

How the law treats risk once a relationship has ended is a recurring argument in British domestic-abuse policy. Separation is widely described by specialist charities and researchers as a period of heightened danger, which is partly why the debate keeps returning to ex-partners specifically.

The law has shifted over the years, often after pressure from families. Controlling or coercive behaviour became a criminal offence in England and Wales under the Serious Crime Act 2015. Stalking protection orders were introduced in 2019. The Domestic Violence Disclosure Scheme, known as Clare's Law, was rolled out nationally in 2014 and takes its name from a woman killed by a former partner. Each of these followed sustained campaigning, and several grew from a single case.

That history is the best guide to what "movement" might lead to. It is also a reason for caution, because a gap often opens between a promise to look at the issue and legislation that reaches the statute book. The interval is frequently measured in years.

## What to watch

Three things will show how far this has gone. The first is whether a minister puts a commitment on the record, in Parliament or in a formal statement, in place of private reassurance to the family. The second is whether the change is attached to a vehicle that already exists, such as a crime or policing bill, which would make it far quicker, or left to a standalone proposal. The third is how the family and the specialist domestic-abuse charities respond to the detail once it is published, since they will judge whether it addresses the risk the campaign was set up to confront.

Until the specifics are public, the story is one of intent and not of law. The test will be whether the signs the family has been given turn into text that can be debated, amended and passed.
family-campaign-law-change.in_one_sentence: A bereaved family's UK campaign over killings by former partners has won early signs of government movement toward a law change, though the exact change is not yet clear.

lockhart-quits-dup.headline: Carla Lockhart quits DUP over Drumcree row
lockhart-quits-dup.body_md:
Carla Lockhart, the MP for Upper Bann, has left the Democratic Unionist Party, according to the edition's reporting, after a fortnight of strain over the Drumcree parade dispute and the party's course at Stormont. The weeks before her exit are well documented. The final step is the part this piece could not independently confirm.

## How the row built

Drumcree, on the edge of Portadown in her constituency, is the site of Northern Ireland's longest-running Orange Order parade dispute. Orangemen have been barred from walking the Garvaghy Road section of their traditional route since the late 1990s. This autumn the dispute flared again, with a rally in Portadown in support of the Drumcree Orangemen and renewed argument over what unionist politicians should do about it.

On 23 October Lockhart said she was stepping down from an internal DUP role. The disagreement was over whether the party should pull Emma Little-Pengelly, the deputy First Minister, out of the power-sharing executive. Lockhart argued that the DUP "can do no other than remove Michelle O'Neill" as First Minister. DUP party officers met on 29 October amid the fall-out.

By 30 October the leader, Gavin Robinson, was publicly saying he did not want her to go. "Well, I hope that's not the case," he told BBC Radio Ulster when asked about speculation she would leave. In a five-page letter to colleagues, Lockhart had called the DUP her "home", something she "greatly values". She said she would set out her path "early next week". The Irish News said a split looked increasingly likely after the Traditional Unionist Voice leader, Jim Allister, praised her.

## What it does and does not change

The Westminster arithmetic is modest. The DUP won five Commons seats in 2024. If Lockhart keeps her seat but sits outside the party, its bloc falls to four. That is a loss of standing more than of votes: the DUP's MPs have not been decisive in a House where Labour holds a large majority.

The pressure falls mainly on Stormont and on unionism. Lockhart's argument, that the DUP should collapse or quit the executive over O'Neill's position, puts her to the party's right. Her path from here will show whether it is a one-person exit or the start of a drift towards the TUV. She may also face questions in Upper Bann over whether voters elected her as a DUP candidate. Nothing in the reporting so far suggests she intends to give up the seat.

## What to watch

Two things will show how far this travels: whether other DUP representatives, particularly councillors in the Portadown area, follow her; and whether Robinson changes the party's line on the executive. Lockhart's own account of where she will sit in the Commons is the next marker.

*Editor's note: reporting available to this desk confirmed the dispute, her resignation from a party post and the speculation up to 30 October. The final departure is as reported in the edition's source, BBC Politics, and should be checked against it.*

florida-jet-crash-breakup.headline: Plane may have broken apart before deadly Florida jet crash, investigators say
florida-jet-crash-breakup.body_md:
US investigators say a business jet that crashed in South Florida on Sunday may have started to come apart in the air before it hit the ground. The accident killed all nine people on board. The finding is early and the cause is undetermined. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has also said weather will be a major focus of its inquiry.

## What investigators have said

The aircraft was a Learjet 60. It crashed in a residential area of Greenacres, in Palm Beach County, about 11km south-west of West Palm Beach. Video posted online shows it striking the ground beside a busy road and exploding. The jet had left Austin, Texas, bound for North Eleuthera in the Bahamas. Two crew and seven passengers were aboard.

Tom Chapman, the NTSB member leading the briefing, said investigators had found evidence that the aircraft began breaking up before impact, and that debris could be widely scattered. He did not say which parts were involved or what the evidence was. He said recovery would be a "daunting challenge" because the impact crater has filled with rainwater.

The wording is cautious, and it matters. "Evidence" of breakup is not a finding of structural failure, and the NTSB has not said what caused the aircraft to come apart, if it did. An airframe can break up because a defect or fatigue weakened it. It can also break up because it was overstressed by something else, such as extreme speed or turbulence.

## The flight's final minutes

Air traffic control recordings captured by the LiveATC.net website, as reported by ABC News (Australia), give a partial picture. The pilot reported ice building on the aircraft and turbulence that jolted it by as much as 700 feet. He first described the ice as light and the turbulence as moderate, then asked to climb about 2,000 feet.

The jet then lost height rapidly. The pilot declared an emergency and reported a descent of 10,000 feet a minute. He later reported an overspeed condition at 20,000 feet a minute. Other video shows the aircraft banking sharply to the right before impact.

These details point in two directions. Ice, turbulence and an uncontrolled dive are a plausible route to loading the airframe beyond its limits, which would make the breakup a consequence of the upset rather than its origin. An aviation safety expert quoted by the BBC suggested that key parts of the tail may have been lost in the turbulence or during the dive. The sequence can only be settled by working out which parts separated first, and at what altitude.

## Who was on board

The dead included the copilot, Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, 20, who earned her pilot's licence in 2023 while still at school. Her licence carried a rating for the Learjet model but not for commanding the flight. Also killed were the technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp and their children, Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2. The other victims were Rachael Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina, the family's nanny. The operator has not been named in the reports reviewed.

About 600 residents of almost 80 mobile homes near the site have been sheltered. Joel Flores, a Palm Beach County commissioner, said the county did not know when they could return home. One man leaving the area in a vehicle suffered a leg injury.

## What to watch

The aircraft was originally fitted with a cockpit voice recorder, and investigators hope to recover it. Its condition, together with the wreckage map, will show whether the breakup came before or after the loss of control. The NTSB usually issues a preliminary report within about 30 days. That report would be the first formal statement of what was found. A probable-cause finding typically takes a year or more. Any inspection orders for the Learjet 60 fleet, or action directed at the operator, would depend on evidence of a structural fault rather than weather damage. No such evidence has been made public.

cyber-freezers-ai-malware-warning.headline: Cyber-attack hits shop freezers in seven European countries as UK warns of AI-enabled malware by 2028
cyber-freezers-ai-malware-warning.body_md:
A cyber-attack on the software that runs commercial refrigeration has hit shops across Europe. BBC reports put the number of affected countries at seven. The attack stopped fridges and freezers from keeping food cold, and it reached well beyond the one chain or one country where the damage first surfaced. The same week, a UK government cyber assessment was reported to say that AI-enabled attacks on critical systems are "highly likely" by 2028. The two stories are separate, but both are about how much everyday infrastructure sits on connected systems that were not built with attackers in mind.

Several details below are not yet confirmed. The BBC's seven-country count could not be matched to a published country list. The attacker has not been established. The 2028 wording comes from press coverage rather than a primary document.

## What happened to the freezers

The earliest detailed reporting that could be found dates from mid-October and centres on France. According to Al Jazeera and other outlets, hundreds of French supermarkets saw fridges and freezers pushed to temperatures as high as 50°C. Food was spoiled and, in some cases, fires started. Chains named in the reports include E.Leclerc, Intermarché, Carrefour, Monoprix and Coopérative U.

The method, as reported, was not brute force against each store. One account says the attackers remotely triggered a forced defrost. Another says the defrost cycle was stretched from one hour to eight, which would also have kept alarms from sounding. Either way, the attacker used the refrigeration controls as they were designed to work, and the stock cooked as a result.

French authorities reportedly identified a flaw in software from the Danish firm Danfoss. The security firm Claroty had published research in August describing vulnerabilities in Danfoss systems that could let an attacker bypass authentication. Whether the attackers used that exact flaw has not been confirmed in the sources checked. France's cyber agency told companies to disconnect the equipment from the internet or restrict access to it, and to apply software updates.

## Across borders

A Sekoia analyst said other European countries were affected, including Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium. Another report named only Spain, Portugal, Germany and Belgium. Added to France, those lists give five or six countries, not seven. The BBC's figure may reflect later reporting, and the exact list should be treated as unsettled.

The spread is itself informative. Supermarket groups differ, but many use the same controller makers and the same remote-management arrangements. A flaw in one widely used product can therefore be exploited in several countries at once without the attacker needing to target each chain individually.

Attribution is murky. One outlet attributed the attack to the group Scattered Spider using DragonForce ransomware. Other reporting says it is not known who was behind it. Without a published investigation, that claim should be treated as unproven.

## The UK forecast

Separately, the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), part of GCHQ, published an assessment of how AI will change the threat. Press coverage, including the Irish News, reports that it judges it highly likely that by 2028 AI tools will be used to exploit known weaknesses in older technology across critical national infrastructure.

The NCSC document located in this search, "Impact of AI on cyber threat from now to 2027", is more cautious in places. It says AI will almost certainly keep making parts of intrusion operations more effective and efficient. It also says that, if mitigations lag, there is "a realistic possibility of critical systems becoming more vulnerable to advanced threat actors by 2027". The phrase "AI-powered malware" in the original brief could not be traced to the NCSC's own text, so it should be read as the newspaper's shorthand.

The NCSC's chief executive, Richard Horne, has said that about 75% of the more than 200 incidents affecting UK critical infrastructure over the past year could be linked to state actors, and that adversaries are pre-positioning inside technology that underpins that infrastructure.

## What links the two

The freezer attack did not involve AI, and nothing found so far suggests it did. The link is the target. The forecast concerns old systems with known flaws, and the Danfoss case fits that pattern: a vulnerability was publicly described in August, and the damage came in October. AI tools matter in the NCSC's reasoning because they could shrink the time between a flaw becoming known and being exploited. That is an argument about speed, and a refrigerator controller on a shop's network is a plausible example of equipment where patches arrive slowly.

The practical lessons so far are modest. Keep operational equipment off the open internet, patch it, and know which vendor's software sits behind which store. Those are the steps France's agency recommended after the attack.

The next markers are an official account of the attack from French and European agencies, including the confirmed country list, the vulnerability used and the attacker. Retailers' loss figures should follow. On the UK side, the NCSC's full 2028 judgement, and any sector-specific guidance that follows it, will show how much of the forecast is a planning assumption and how much is a warning about specific systems.

cps-ai-fake-case-high-court.headline: CPS prosecutor cited imaginary case in High Court after AI search
cps-ai-fake-case-high-court.body_md:
A lawyer for the Crown Prosecution Service put two court authorities in front of the High Court that do not exist. The CPS now says generative AI was probably where they came from. The errors were caught before the hearing and changed nothing in the outcome. They still got into a judgment, because the judge decided a mistake of this kind needed to be on the record.

The judgment, reported as [2026] EWHC 1720 (Admin), was covered by legal trade outlets in July 2026. The wording is cited from those reports. A single Guardian report was the prompt for this piece, and it could not be located, so its exact phrasing, including the description of the lapse as 'a serious failure', could not be confirmed. That phrase does not appear in the reports checked.

## What happened

The case was a pair of extradition appeals brought by Romanian nationals, reported by Law360 under the name Tobosaru v Court of Law Craiova. The CPS acted for the Romanian authorities. Two cited cases appeared in its grounds of opposition, prepared the year before. They were then carried forward into a document headed 'Respondent submissions'.

They got past the permission stage. They were not relied on in the February skeleton argument, but that document did not say they had already been identified as unreliable. The CPS first gave the court an account suggesting the appellants' counsel had spotted the problem. It later corrected that and apologised twice. Both appeals were rejected.

## What the CPS and the judge said

The CPS told the court the 'operative cause was human error in the failure to verify the authorities relied upon'. It said generative AI may have been the immediate source, and it stressed that this was not a deliberate attempt to mislead. The tool was not named in the reports.

A Chief Crown Prosecutor told the court that a full internal review had been carried out. Senior managers went through 78 other cases handled by the same lawyer and found no similar problems.

Mr Justice Sweeting accepted the apology. He set out what happened 'given the serious consequences that an error of this nature might have had in other circumstances'. He added that the episode 'highlights the risks of its use without appropriate oversight particularly for legal research'. Legal Futures noted that he did not appear to apply the *Ayinde* guidance, the earlier High Court warning about fake citations, in deciding whether to take further action.

## Why it matters

Fake citations from AI tools have turned up in court filings before, mostly from individual litigants and private practitioners. This one involved the state prosecution service, which handles a large volume of work, and the lawyer's own caseload had to be audited as a result.

The CPS's own explanation is the useful part. It blames a missing check, not the software. A lawyer who files an authority vouches for it, whatever produced it, and a search tool that can invent a case does not change that duty. It does make the check unavoidable: every citation has to be looked up in a primary source before it goes into a filing.

The CPS says it has reminded its lawyers of their duties as officers of the court, reviewed its processes and shared the lessons across the organisation. Whether that is enough is open. The reports show no further sanction, and the next test will be whether another filing, from the CPS or anyone else, brings the same problem back before a court.
cps-ai-fake-case-high-court.in_one_sentence: The CPS put two non-existent cases before the High Court, probably from generative AI; the judge accepted its apology but recorded the episode and warned of unsupervised AI research.

apple-foldable-sells-out.headline: Apple's first foldable iPhone sells out, with no date for restocking
apple-foldable-sells-out.body_md:
Apple's first foldable iPhone has sold out, and the company has not said when more will be available. The iPhone Duo went on pre-order on 16 October at $1,999. Launch stock was gone within minutes. Delivery estimates for every colour and storage option moved to January almost immediately. Apple's US store was showing 25 January about half an hour after orders opened, according to reports.

The BBC reported that Apple cannot give a date for resupply. That leaves two possible explanations. Either buyers wanted more phones than Apple planned for, or Apple could not make as many as it hoped. The reporting so far points mostly to the second.

## What happened at launch

The Duo was unveiled in September. It has a 5.4-inch outer screen that opens into a 7.6-inch inner display. Pre-orders opened at 8am New York time on Friday 16 October, and the phone went on sale on 23 October. Storage runs from 256GB to 2TB, and the top model costs $3,199, according to AppleInsider as cited by The Next Web.

Bloomberg reported that stock sold out at Apple's own stores almost as soon as pre-orders began. Apple normally holds some phones back for walk-in customers on launch day. This time it said only that it would have "limited" numbers in stores. Reports from launch day described queues turned away before the doors opened, and Apple reportedly told stores to warn walk-in customers off.

Apple has called demand "outstanding" but has not said how many phones it had to sell. It has also not said when supply will recover. The January dates are Apple's own delivery estimates for online orders, not a restocking commitment. They may also apply mainly to the US. I found no Apple statement promising a single shipping date across every market.

## Demand or supply?

A sell-out on its own cannot tell the two explanations apart. Several things in the pre-launch reporting favour a supply problem.

- **The hinge.** Analyst Jeff Pu cut his 2026 Duo shipment forecast from 7 million to 6 million in September. He blamed hinge constraints, not weak demand. Counterpoint Research, per Bloomberg, also expects about 6 million units this year.
- **The panel.** Korea JoongAng Daily reports that Samsung Display is the sole supplier of foldable panels for the Duo. Chinese outlet Jiemian News, citing supply-chain sources, reported low yields, delayed deliveries and design changes at Samsung Display. It also reported that assembly yield at Foxconn sat just above 60%, partly because the panel delays left less time to tune final assembly. Apple has not commented on any of this.
- **Apple's own foreknowledge.** Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported that Apple knew supply would be severely constrained and opened pre-orders in more than 70 countries anyway. Analyst Ming-Chi Kuo had said in July that the phone could sell out immediately and leave long waits.

The unit numbers come largely from one analyst and anonymous supply-chain sources, so they are estimates. For scale, Pu's note put iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max shipments at about 12 times his Duo estimate. A phone planned at 6 million units is a small product by Apple's standards, and a small run can sell out quickly even if demand is only moderately strong.

That does not rule out strong demand. Foldables have been a niche part of the smartphone market, and an Apple entry may draw buyers who were waiting for it. But a sell-out that was expected in advance says little about whether the product is a hit. The better test is whether demand holds once supply catches up in 2027.

## Who else is affected

The supplier angle matters beyond Apple. If Samsung Display is the only panel source, as reported, a yield problem there becomes an Apple problem. A strong Duo would also boost a company that already competes with Apple in phones.

Apple is also trying to move faster. John Ternus became chief executive on 1 September, and The Next Web reports he has been cutting management layers to ship products sooner. A first-generation product that cannot be bought for three months is an awkward test of that. Apple's shares rose 1.8% in pre-market trading on the day pre-orders opened, so investors read the sell-out as good news.

## What to watch

The first signal is whether Apple's delivery estimates move beyond late January, or shorten. The second is Apple's next quarterly report, where it may say something about foldable supply. The third is any word from Samsung Display on panel yields. If estimates improve without new capacity being announced, the problem was a launch bottleneck. If they keep slipping, the Duo's supply chain is the limit on the whole foldable category, and demand may matter less than whether Apple can build enough phones.
apple-foldable-sells-out.in_one_sentence: Apple's first foldable iPhone, the $1,999 iPhone Duo, sold out within minutes and Apple gives no restock date; reporting points to hinge and panel constraints more than a demand surprise.

physics-smallest-scale-signals.headline: Scientists report signals at the smallest scale yet explored
physics-smallest-scale-signals.body_md:
Physicists at the Large Hadron Collider have reported seeing the effects of physics at a distance of about a billionth of a trillionth of a metre (10⁻²¹ m), roughly 100 billion times smaller than an atom. The finding was first reported by the BBC on 3 November. The scale is the smallest yet probed by experiment, according to the researchers. Nothing new has been found at it, and the claim is more modest than the headline suggests.

## What was done

The LHC, at CERN on the Swiss-French border, smashes particles together at very high energy. Researchers then study the debris. This team, led from the University of Cambridge, looked at a beauty quark, an unstable particle that decays after about 1.5 trillionths of a second. Despite that brief life, the team detected it interacting with other tiny particles.

The logic is indirect. Quantum theory lets short-lived, unseen particles influence how a quark decays, even when they are too heavy to be made directly. A tiny shift in a decay rate or pattern can therefore carry information about distances far smaller than any microscope could resolve. Some physicists call this regime the "zeptoverse".

Dr Harry Cliff, who led the data analysis, put it this way: "We're knocking on the door of this zeptoverse." He added that more data is needed to find any new particles. So the report is of sensitivity to this scale, not of a discovery there.

## What is not yet clear

The BBC article, as reproduced by Yahoo, does not name a journal or paper, so the result's peer-review status is unclear. It links the work to the LHCb detector's planned upgrade and quotes the LHCb collaboration leader, but it never explicitly names LHCb as the source of the data. Those gaps matter. "Smallest scale ever explored" is a claim about the reach of a measurement, and it can only be judged against the paper's own uncertainties and earlier limits.

The dark matter angle is also a possibility, not a result. Some theories hold that particles at this scale could be more sensitive to dark matter, which makes up much of the universe but is seen only through its gravity. If so, the effects might show up in how quarks interact and decay. No dark matter detection is reported.

## Money, and who gets to look

The more concrete news in the story is about funding. The 28 member countries have agreed a £150m upgrade to the LHCb detector, which would raise the rate of these decays tenfold. UK Research and Innovation has said it will withdraw its share, as part of cuts that also affect Jodrell Bank's Lovell telescope.

Prof Tim Gershon, who leads the LHCb collaboration, warned: "The UK is at risk of not being involved and making really major discoveries." Dr Mary Richardson-Slipper, part of the Cambridge team, said she is considering jobs abroad because of better opportunities there. Prof Brian Cox, who was not involved, called the result "important" but criticised the funding cut. UKRI says it remains a fully engaged CERN member and its second-largest funder, at about £175m a year.

## What to watch

The first marker is the paper itself: its venue, its statistical significance and how the claimed scale is defined. The second is the upgrade. A tenfold rise in decays would show whether the faint effects hold up or fade, and the UK's decision on its share will determine who is in the room when the data arrive.
physics-smallest-scale-signals.in_one_sentence: LHC physicists report sensitivity to physics at about 10⁻²¹ metres, the smallest scale yet probed, but no new particle has been found and the paper's status is unclear.

russell-brand-trial-defence.headline: Russell Brand trial: defence says he is not a 'psychopath who rapes people'
russell-brand-trial-defence.body_md:
Russell Brand's defence team has begun its closing case to the jury at Southwark Crown Court, telling jurors that the comedian is not, in the words of the headline claim, a "psychopath who rapes people". It is the last stage of a trial that has become a contest over two competing portraits of the man: a serial predator who treated women as "disposable", or a famous, promiscuous man whose many sexual encounters were consensual.

*A note on sourcing: the "psychopath" phrasing comes from the triage summary. Reports available at the time of writing covered the prosecution's closing and the run-up to the defence speech, but did not carry the defence barrister's words, so the line is not quoted directly here.*

## The charges

Brand, 51, denies seven counts: three of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault. They involve six women, and the alleged offences span 1999 to 2009. The trial opened on 12 October, and the jury must reach a unanimous verdict on each count. The judge said at the outset that the trial was expected to last about six weeks.

## Two portraits

The prosecution closed on Friday 30 October. Riel Karmy-Jones KC told jurors that women "as a whole were disposable; they didn't matter to him". She described Brand's defence as "a lot of half-truths, but spun into lies", and argued that the six complainants had "nothing to gain" by coming forward and had not been swayed by media coverage. She also said Brand's account was built around the details the accusers had given, and that he "couldn't really remember anything" when interviewed by police.

The defence case is that every encounter was consensual. Brand gave evidence for about four hours, called by his barrister, Ian Winter KC. He told the court "I'm innocent" and described the allegations as devastating. He also made concessions that cut both ways: he admitted he had been wrong to use his fame in pursuit of sex, saying "regrettably I've had a lot of consensual sex, which I see has caused harm", and acknowledged small inconsistencies in his recollection. He said no one with relevant information had agreed to testify for him. Those admissions give the defence a way to argue that a man who is candid about his flaws is not the monster described.

That is the logic of the argument that he is no "psychopath". It does not dispute that Brand behaved badly by many standards; it contests the leap from careless, fame-fuelled promiscuity to criminal predation. The jury is being asked to decide whether the prosecution's portrait is a fair inference from the evidence or a caricature.

## What the verdict will test

The case rests heavily on credibility. The events are decades old, the complainants' accounts are set against Brand's, and the arguments on both sides have turned on memory, motive and the weight to give inconsistencies. A verdict will show how a jury treats historic allegations against a high-profile figure, and how much a complainant's imperfect recall, or a defendant's partial admissions, counts for.

The jury is expected to retire to consider its verdicts after the judge sums up, possibly within days. The trial is due to conclude this week.

moyes-grealish-everton-future.headline: Moyes says Grealish can still have an Everton future
moyes-grealish-everton-future.body_md:
David Moyes has said Jack Grealish can still have a future at Everton. It is a signal about squad planning, not a decision, and the available detail stops there.

The Everton manager's comments, reported by BBC Sport, concern the winger's prospects at the club. The wording of the remarks, and whether Moyes was answering a direct question about Grealish's contract or his place in the side, has not been independently confirmed. This article therefore does not quote him.

## What the comment does and doesn't say

Managers asked about a player's future tend to leave doors open, and "can still have a future" is a long way from "will be offered a deal". Nothing in the reporting available here suggests Moyes has fixed a course for Grealish, whether that means a new contract, an extension of his stay or a parting of the ways. The phrasing points to a manager keeping his options open rather than closing them.

Grealish arrived at Goodison Park as a high-profile addition, and his status shapes how Everton plan their wage bill and attacking options. The terms of his stay, including whether Everton hold any option to keep him, are the context that would turn this from a pleasantry into a story. They have not been verified, so they are not set out here.

## Barry's revival

The second thread is Barry. The candidate summary says only that his revival is also in focus, which most plausibly means the forward is finding form after a quieter spell. That is an inference from the summary, not a confirmed account. Any detail on his goals, minutes or the manager's own assessment awaits the full BBC Sport report.

The two themes fit together. A forward rediscovering his touch gives Moyes more attacking choices, and that tends to sharpen questions about who else belongs in the squad, and on what terms.

## What to watch

The clearest signal will be a concrete one: Grealish's starts and minutes in the coming league fixtures, and any word from the club on his contract situation. Until Moyes or Everton put a decision on the record, this remains a manager speaking warmly about a player, which is worth noting but not worth over-reading.

melbourne-cup-kings-former-horse.headline: King's former horse wins the Melbourne Cup
melbourne-cup-kings-former-horse.body_md:
A three-year-old colt sold out of the royal string earlier this year has won the Melbourne Cup. Point of Law, bred in England and owned until recently by King Charles III and Queen Camilla, took the 3,200-metre handicap at Flemington on Tuesday by 3.75 lengths.

It was a fine day for the Maher stable. Ciaron Maher trained the first three home, with Point of Law ahead of stablemates Zahrann and Juja Kibo. It is his second Melbourne Cup win. Ethan Brown, the winning jockey, claimed his first.

## From Windsor to Flemington

The royal link is confirmed by ABC News, which describes Point of Law as "formerly owned by King Charles III and Queen Camilla". Its separate Cup roundup says the King "sold the colt earlier this year" to a consortium of Australians. It names one member: Chris Judd, the former West Coast and Carlton star.

The detail is thinner than the headline. ABC gives no exact sale date, price or method. Other outlets give differing months for the sale, so the timing is best left at "earlier this year". Maher thanked "the owners" after the race without naming them, and the rest of the syndicate has not been identified in the reports checked. No reaction from the King or the Palace had been reported at the time of writing.

The colt is a Northern Hemisphere three-year-old, and the Cup was only his sixth start. A young European import, sold on to Australian buyers and then asked to see out two miles in the country's biggest race, is a well-worn route to the Cup. Winning it with a horse bred and raced for the monarch is less usual.

## The race that stops a nation

The Melbourne Cup is run on the first Tuesday of November, a date that closes offices and fills Flemington. Its nickname, "the race that stops a nation", is only a mild exaggeration. For the royal racing operation, which is run with a long-term breeding eye rather than a sales one, the result carries a certain wryness: the prize went to the buyers.

ABC's roundup could not resist the obvious speculation about how the late Queen Elizabeth II, a devoted owner-breeder, might have taken her son selling a horse that went on to win the Cup. Whatever the answer, the sale will be remembered at least as well as the win.

## What next

Two things are worth watching. One is the identity of the full ownership group and what Point of Law is now worth, since a Cup winner's value rises sharply. The other is whether the Palace says anything about the sale. Maher's plans for the colt, including whether he stays in Australia or returns to Europe, have not been announced.

royal-mail-christmas-stamps-2026.headline: Royal Mail unveils its Christmas 2026 stamps
royal-mail-christmas-stamps-2026.body_md:
Royal Mail has put its Christmas 2026 stamps on sale, the latest entry in a calendar fixture that arrives every autumn. The issue was reported by BBC UK and appears in Royal Mail's own 2026 stamp calendar under today's date, 3 November.

The release is the only fact in the brief that has been confirmed. Published details of this year's designs, the artists and the denominations were not available when this piece was prepared, so none are described here. Anyone wanting the images will find them on royalmail.com, at Post Office branches and in the Royal Mail app, which is where last year's set was sold.

## A fixture of the calendar

The Christmas issue is one of the most predictable events in British philately. Royal Mail publishes its special-issue programme a year ahead, and the Christmas stamps come last, in early November, in time for the card-writing season. The 2026 calendar sits alongside other issues this year, from Military Jet Aircraft to Football.

Last year's set offered a useful comparison. The 2025 issue ran to five stamps with Nativity-themed designs by Paula Doherty. Royal Mail also sold them in collectible formats, including a souvenir stamp sheet. The pattern is a small set of stamps for the cards and a range of keepsakes for collectors.

## The practical date

More useful than the artwork may be the postal deadline. Royal Mail's Christmas page says last posting dates for 2026 are now available. A third-party site puts the last recommended second-class date at Friday 18 December. That has not been checked against Royal Mail's own guide, and anyone relying on it should consult the company's guidance first.

## Why it is only a brief

There is little market consequence in a stamp launch. A fuller story would need figures that the release does not supply. They would cover Christmas parcel and letter volumes, the effect of falling letter traffic on the business, and the position of the company's owner, International Distribution Services, which is controlled by the Czech billionaire Daniel Kretinsky's EP Group. None of those is established by this announcement, and the brief makes no claim about them.

What to watch next is the posting deadlines. They fall in mid-December, and the company's own guide is the source to check.

h5n1-indiana-dairy-herd.headline: H5N1 confirmed in another Indiana dairy herd
h5n1-indiana-dairy-herd.body_md:
The US Department of Agriculture has confirmed highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 in a dairy herd in Indiana. The detection was announced on 2 November and is the state's first in cattle. The headline's "another" is therefore slightly off: this is a new state for the outbreak, not a repeat. Indiana's own animal-health board reported in its August situation update that it had not diagnosed the disease in livestock. Its 2026 cases had been in poultry, mostly commercial duck operations in LaGrange County.

## What the USDA has said

The National Veterinary Services Laboratories confirmed the infection by PCR testing. The virus belongs to genotype B3.13, the lineage tied to the cattle outbreak since it was first identified in March 2024. The herd was found through routine sampling under the National Milk Testing Strategy, not through pre-movement testing of animals bound for sale. That matters. It suggests the surveillance programme is catching infections that nobody had flagged by clinical signs, though the release does not say whether the animals were showing illness.

The agency's release leaves several things unstated. It does not name the county or give the herd's size. It does not say how the virus arrived. One aggregator, which cites the release, reports Newton County. The release itself, as retrieved, names no county, so that detail should be treated as unconfirmed. Nor did the USDA say whether other herds are under investigation. The Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service said it is working with the Indiana State Board of Animal Health on on-farm investigations, diagnostic testing and the collection of epidemiological data. It added that the detection does not change its eradication strategy.

Indiana's response plan, published by the state board, calls for a quarantine on lactating cattle on the affected premises and a 10-kilometre surveillance zone around it. Whether those measures have been invoked here has not been reported.

## Why this one is more than a routine update

On its own, one herd is a small event. The context is what lifts it. The USDA says dairy cattle in 21 states have now been infected since March 2024, and it notes recent cases in previously unaffected states. Colorado has reported its first infected herd in nearly two years. Washington state, where the virus was confirmed in two Yakima County herds on 8 October, reported six more on 30 October. That brought its total to 40 herds, nearly all in Yakima County.

The Washington outbreak has also had a human cost. The Yakima Health District said a county resident who had been exposed to infected dairy cattle died of avian influenza on 1 November. The person had an underlying health condition, and the district withheld their name, age and sex. Capital Press reported it as the third US death from the virus and the first following exposure on a dairy farm. "While this is a serious and heartbreaking outcome, the risk to the general public remains low," the district's health officer, Dave Atteberry, said.

Nothing published links the Indiana herd to Washington. The two are separated by roughly 2,000 miles, and genotype B3.13 is not specific to either. The Washington article did not name a genotype, so even that comparison cannot be drawn from available reporting. Linking the cases would take sequencing and animal-movement tracing that has not yet been released.

## Safety of milk and risk to people

The Food and Drug Administration says pasteurisation inactivates the virus, and the USDA says milk from affected animals is diverted or destroyed so it does not enter the food supply. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention continues to rate the risk to the general public as low. People with occupational or recreational exposure to infected animals face higher risk and are advised to follow CDC precautions, including protective equipment.

## What to watch

The next indicators are concrete. The first is whether the USDA's livestock dashboard lists the Indiana herd and any further Indiana herds, and in which counties. The second is whether state testing of neighbouring dairies turns up more positives, which would suggest local spread beyond a single introduction. The third is whether sequencing ties the herd to a known cattle lineage or to a fresh spillover from wild birds, as in the Wisconsin case reported last December. Any of those would change this from a one-herd addition to a sign of wider spread.

newcastle-jaissle-home-jeers.headline: Jaissle faces growing home problems at Newcastle as jeers return
newcastle-jaissle-home-jeers.body_md:
Matthias Jaissle has been at Newcastle for little more than two months, and the St James' Park crowd has already started to let him know what it thinks. The jeers that followed the 1-0 defeat by Aston Villa in mid-October were the first sign that the honeymoon for the club's new head coach is over. BBC Sport reports they have returned as home form has soured.

The caveat is that the evidence available is thin. The record below runs to mid-October. A fixture list shows Newcastle hosting Everton on 2 November, but no result for that game could be confirmed, so the picture since the Villa loss is incomplete.

## A good start, then two defeats

It began well enough. Jaissle's first home game, against Liverpool on 23 August, finished 2-2 after Dominik Szoboszlai scored a penalty in the ninth minute of stoppage time. Jaissle called the award "soft" and said it had cost him a winning debut. A 2-0 win over Tottenham followed, then a 1-1 draw with Bournemouth in which his side came from behind.

Then came two defeats in five days. Coventry City won 4-1 on 12 October. Five days later Villa won 1-0 at St James' Park, a first home loss of the season and the first of Jaissle's tenure. By one account, Villa should have led by more at half-time. Newcastle stayed 11th, and the boos followed the final whistle.

One listing puts the club on 8 points from seven games, 13 behind leaders Manchester City. That source could not be cross-checked, and a second table gave inconsistent figures, so the numbers are best treated as approximate.

## Why the home crowd matters here

St James' Park has long been the club's main asset. Newcastle finished 12th last season, and 32 of their 49 points came at home. A team that cannot hold that ground is not going to climb the table. Supporters also know what a lively home crowd can deliver, which is part of why the patience runs short when it does not.

Reports on the Villa defeat questioned the 4-2-3-1 system Jaissle has favoured, and said patience was running thin. It is a familiar early-tenure complaint: a new coach's structure is judged against the results before the squad has fully adapted to it. Jaissle's reaction after the Villa game was conciliatory rather than defensive. He said he understood the supporters' frustration and that the players shared it.

The jeers have another edge. Newcastle fans have had a busy few months of emotion, not least the hostile reception for Alexander Isak on his return with Liverpool. Booing a departed striker is one thing. Booing your own side is a different, more worrying signal.

## What comes next

No one is calling for Jaissle's job on this evidence, and two defeats do not make a crisis. The real test is the next run of home fixtures. Another dropped home match would turn the jeers from a mood into a pattern, and would give the board a decision to weigh. A win would quieten St James' Park quickly. It usually does.

floor.body_md: Quiet names, loud result. Four of the five positions in the uk-eu mean-reverter book closed green, but the day belonged to one. MCARY had sold off hard on its own, with no sector move behind it, and it snapped back quickly enough that the midday take-profit fired before the twenty-day average came into view. The exit took most of the reversion rather than holding out for the moving average, which is the discipline the thesis needs. TSQ and ZEPP followed a smaller version of the same script. DGSE.SW was the odd one out: it closed exactly where it started, so the loss is friction, not a verdict on the idea. Strip out MCARY and this is an ordinary session. Tomorrow's question is whether the snap-back repeats in names without a catalyst, or whether this was one good draw.

floor.headline: Five shadow trades, five losses, and a sub-dollar name that never moved
floor.body_md:
Five trades, five losses, and no movement on the one that cost the most.

The ml-challenger's shadow book spent the day showing that a strong-up call is only as good as the price that follows.

BLMH carried the damage. The model expected a sharp rise, but the stock printed the same level at entry and at its scheduled exit, so the thesis never got a chance to be right or wrong. What remains looks like friction on a sub-dollar name, a cost the forecast ignored.

FCUV made the same mistake from a different angle: a gap-up signal with no continuation.

Tomorrow, check whether an overnight-gap call on a thin name expects a move large enough to clear the cost of getting in and out.

floor.headline: Mean-reverter posts a quiet, positive session on three closes
floor.body_md: Mean-reverter, running on the uk-eu shadow book, had a modest but positive session. Three closed positions, in GRI.MC, OXLC and PPGN.SW, added up to £21.15, an average gain of 0.34%. Nothing dramatic here: the strategy traded only a handful of names and booked small gains rather than a single standout move. It is a quiet result, but a positive one, and the names involved are worth tracking as the next batch of closes comes in to see whether the tone holds.

floor.headline: RDDT's -29% ran without us; ASM and ASML were in-universe misses
floor.body_md: RDDT fell 29.2% with no catalyst we could find, and the bot held nothing and cannot short. The more instructive miss is ASM.AS (-7.6%) and ASML.AS (-6.1%): both sit in the AEX 25, which feeds uk_eu_blue_chips, so the "outside any universe" label in today's missed-movers file is wrong. They were screened in and passed over by strategy rules. The same label likely applies to BAYN.DE (+5.5%) and IHG.L (+2.6%), which probably sit in the DAX or FTSE 100 lists (not verified). Two headline numbers are stale: INTC's -28.6% and FDXF's +15.3% both reflect Oct 30 gaps, not Nov 2 moves. GPN (+13.0%, reported takeover interest) is the only US name with a plausible news trigger. The bot held no top mover today, so there is no credit to give.
